This does not make meaning magical; it makes a messy judgment measurable. Once that arrangement exists, a vague request such as find evidence like this claim becomes a concrete operation: compare distances and choose nearby candidates. The price is compression, because a rich object must be squeezed into a limited description and some detail will be lost. The useful hope is that the lost detail is mostly decorative, while the kept detail is what matters for the task. The papers under similarity keep returning to that hope, whether the object is a shopper, an image, a web page, a graph node, a student exercise, a security signal, or a sequence of locations.
similarity.why: Similarity works when nearness in the learned arrangement tracks the kind of sameness the task actually needs. If two products are close because their images, text, and buying behavior agree, a shopper looking at one may plausibly want the other. If two paragraphs are close because they support the same scientific claim, a citation tool can use one to check the other. The mechanism is repeated comparison: examples that should agree are pulled into the same neighborhood, while examples that should not be confused are kept apart. This creates a map where local neighborhoods become evidence, not just decoration. It breaks when the training comparisons reward the wrong kind of likeness, such as popularity instead of relevance, surface wording instead of evidence, or nearby streets instead of a real path. It also breaks when one number or one location is asked to carry too many meanings at once. Several papers respond by separating views, regions, roles, channels, or scales so that visual similarity, text similarity, time similarity, graph-role similarity, and personal-taste similarity do not overwrite each other. The guarantee is therefore practical rather than absolute: closeness is trustworthy only when the data used to build the map reflects the decision the system will later make. The central tradeoff is reach versus faithfulness, because the same map can make search cheap across huge collections, but it can also hide the reason two things were judged close.
similarity.math: The mathematical object is a space where every item is represented by a list of numbers. Each position in that list is not usually a human label; it is a learned coordinate that helps place the item relative to other items. Distance then becomes the main measurement: two lists that are near each other are treated as more alike than two lists that are far apart. The important move is not the distance formula by itself, but the training pressure that decides what near should mean. Multi-view recommendation pulls behavior, images, text, and links toward a common agreement about user-item fit. Cross-modal retrieval maps sketches, descriptions, images, and text into a shared comparison surface so one kind of input can find another kind of output. Graph papers change the shape of the surface when ordinary flat distance is too weak to express hierarchy, roles, communities, or directed links. Time-series papers reorder or compress channels so signals that depend on one another become local enough to compare. Diffusion-style papers start with noisy guesses and repeatedly move them toward cleaner descriptions that preserve domain-specific and domain-general structure. The loss in all of this is that a rich object becomes a point, so the system must decide which differences deserve to survive the squeeze. The payoff is that once the squeeze is learned well, retrieval, ranking, classification, editing, and forecasting can all reuse the same simple act of measuring nearness.
similarity.family: These papers are siblings because they all face the same hidden task: build a usable map before making a decision. Recommendation papers need a map of people, items, images, text, and changing preferences so the next suggestion is not chosen from raw clicks alone. Retrieval papers need a map where a sketch can find an image, a claim can find evidence, a campaign can find a product type, and a scientific paragraph can find a valid reference. Graph papers need a map where nodes are close for the right reason, whether that reason is shared neighborhood, opposite but related role, common cluster, hierarchy, or direction of influence. Forecasting and trajectory papers need a map where nearby past patterns help fill missing places or predict future signal. The repeated failure mode is false sameness: two things look alike on one surface clue but differ in the property that matters. The common move is to compare several views, keep the stable shared signal, and reduce the influence of accidental or decorative similarity. What changes across the group is the object being mapped, not the deeper pressure. The family is therefore about turning messy evidence into a geometry of trust, while admitting that every geometry leaves something out.
similarity.dots: Multi-view Semantic Contrastive Alignment and TargetMR show similarity as agreement across different product evidence: behavior, images, text, links, and central objects must point toward the same item relationships. ARCHER uses the same move in e-commerce search, first aligning broad category likeness and then refining toward specific product differences. SketchMind, MCoT-MVS, and HL-CMR stretch similarity across sketches, generated descriptions, images, and text, so the query and the target need not arrive in the same form. CiteLLM, OwlerLite, EmeraldApp, Campaign-2-PT-RAG, and the LOPE method use nearness to connect claims, pages, evidence chunks, campaign text, or extracted terms to the most relevant support. UTAG, ConceptFormer, C-HyPOD, Learning on Adaptive Manifolds, Node Role-Guided LLMs, VSAL, Dir-GD, and graph explanation work show that graph similarity is not only about shared neighbors; it can mean shared role, hierarchy, cluster membership, visual layout, direction, or compressed structure. Language Model Representations for Few-Shot Tabular Classification and the learner-item cognitive modeling paper use general language-derived descriptions, then adjust them so rows or exercises are close for the task at hand rather than merely close in wording. RAIE divides preference space into regions, because a user's changing taste may be similar to one local group of histories but not to another. Sharpness-Aware Minimization for federated recommendation asks for item descriptions that stay useful when different clients provide uneven data. Trajectory recovery, cross-domain sequential recommendation, microservice forecasting, and channel reordering all turn time or location patterns into neighborhoods where missing or future states can be inferred from related traces. Emotion editing and diffusion-guided knowledge transfer use similarity as a guardrail, moving an output toward a desired change while keeping the content or domain structure that should remain close. Across all of them, the shared move is to decide what kind of closeness deserves trust, build a map that preserves that closeness, and then use nearby cases as candidates, evidence, forecasts, or controlled edits.
similarity.picture: Imagine arranging a workshop so that tools used for the same job sit near one another, even if they look different: sandpaper, clamps, and varnish end up near furniture repair, while a shiny decorative handle stays farther away if it does not help the task. Similarity is that layout learned from use rather than labels. The layout is powerful because you can find the next useful tool by looking nearby, but it fails when the workshop was arranged around the wrong habit.
